unit-1.title: Using Digital Tools
unit-1.description: Using a computer or tablet carefully, creating and saving a simple picture, and using a keyboard.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 -- Using a Computer or Tablet Safely and Carefully
lessons.objectives: Turn a device on and off correctly; carry and use a device carefully; open and close a simple app.
lessons.syllabusRef: Tools and content creation -- Using devices

steps.title: Looking after our devices
steps.definition: A computer or tablet is a tool that needs to be handled carefully -- carried with two hands, kept away from water and food, and turned on and off the correct way.
steps.example: Before starting, we place the tablet flat on the table and press the power button once, instead of tapping the screen many times.

cards.label: Carry with two hands
cards.content: Holding a tablet with two hands stops it slipping and being dropped.

cards.label: Keep away from water and food
cards.content: Spills can break a device, so we keep drinks and food away from it.

cards.label: Tap gently, once
cards.content: One gentle tap is enough -- pressing hard or many times does not make it work faster.

cards.label: Ask before turning on
cards.content: We ask a grown-up or teacher before turning a device on, so they know we are using it.

cards.question: You want to carry a tablet across the room. What should you do?
cards.answer: Carry it carefully with two hands.

cards.question: The screen isn't responding, so you tap it very hard many times. Is this a good idea?
cards.answer: No -- tapping gently once and waiting is better; hard or repeated taps don't help and could damage the screen.

summaryPoints: We carry devices carefully with two hands and keep them away from water and food.
We tap gently and ask a grown-up before turning a device on.
homeworkItems: If there is a tablet, computer, or phone at home, practise carrying it carefully with a grown-up watching.

teachingScript.overview: Model correct handling with a real classroom tablet or computer before children touch one themselves, and physically demonstrate the two-hands carry.

talkingPoints: Show the correct way to carry and place a tablet before explaining why.
Ask children to demonstrate each rule physically as it is revealed.
Discuss why hard or repeated tapping does not help, in simple terms.
Have each child practise turning a device on and off correctly once, with supervision.

quizQuestions.question: How should you carry a tablet?
What should you keep away from a device?

flashcards.definition: A tool like a computer or tablet that we use to do digital tasks.
Doing something slowly and thoughtfully so nothing gets damaged.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Looking After Our Devices
worksheetContent.instructions: Circle the pictures that show a device being used carefully.

questions.prompt: Name one rule for carrying a tablet safely.
Why should we keep drinks away from a computer or tablet?
Draw yourself using a device carefully.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 -- Creating and Saving a Simple Picture
lessons.objectives: Use a simple drawing tool to create a picture; understand what "saving" means and why we do it.
lessons.syllabusRef: Tools and content creation -- Creating content

steps.title: Making and saving a picture
steps.definition: We can use a simple drawing tool on a computer or tablet to make a picture, just like drawing on paper. Saving a picture means the computer remembers it, so we can find it and look at it again later.
steps.example: After drawing a picture of a fish, we tap the save button so the picture doesn't disappear when the tablet is turned off.

steps.label: Open the drawing tool
steps.detail: Tap the drawing app icon to open a blank page.

steps.label: Choose a colour and draw
steps.detail: Tap a colour, then use your finger or a stylus to draw a picture.

steps.label: Give it a name
steps.detail: Type a simple name for the picture, like "my-fish".

steps.label: Save it
steps.detail: Tap the save button so the picture is kept and can be opened again later.

questions.question: What does "saving" a picture mean?
options: Making the computer remember it for later
questions.feedback: ✓ Saving keeps the picture so we can find it again.

questions.question: What should you do after finishing a drawing?
options: Turn the device off straight away
questions.feedback: ✓ Saving first means the drawing won't be lost.

summaryPoints: We can use a drawing tool to create a simple picture on a device.
Saving a picture means the computer remembers it, so we don't lose our work.
homeworkItems: Tell a grown-up what picture you would like to draw and save next time you use a device.

teachingScript.overview: Give each child (or pair) hands-on time with a real simple drawing app so "saving" is an action they perform themselves, not just a word they hear.

talkingPoints: Compare saving on a device to keeping a paper drawing safe in a folder.
Demonstrate the four steps live on a screen the whole class can see before children try it themselves.
misconceptions: Children may think a drawing is automatically kept without saving -- clarify that many apps need an explicit save step.

talkingPoints: Ask children to explain in their own words what would happen if they forgot to save.
Let each child briefly show their saved picture to a partner.

quizQuestions.question: What tool can we use to make a simple picture on a device?
Why do we save our picture?
options: So the computer remembers it for later

flashcards.definition: To make the computer remember something, like a picture, so it can be opened again later.
A simple app used to create pictures on a computer or tablet.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Creating and Saving a Picture
worksheetContent.instructions: Answer the questions about making and saving a picture.

questions.prompt: What do we call an app we use to draw pictures on a device?
Why is it important to save a picture before turning off a device?
questions.answer: So the picture is not lost and can be opened again later.

questions.prompt: Draw a picture of something you would like to create and save on a computer.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 -- Typing and Using a Keyboard
lessons.objectives: Recognise the letter keys and space bar on a keyboard; type your own name carefully.
lessons.syllabusRef: Tools and content creation -- Using devices

steps.title: Using a keyboard
steps.definition: A keyboard has keys for every letter and number, plus a long space bar for adding a space between words. Typing means pressing keys one at a time to write words on a screen.
steps.example: To type your name "Ana", you find and press the A key, then the N key, then the A key again.

cards.label: Letter keys
cards.content: Each key has one letter -- press it once to type that letter.

cards.label: Space bar
cards.content: The long key at the bottom adds a space between words.

cards.label: Backspace
cards.content: This key removes the last letter you typed, in case of a mistake.

cards.label: Enter key
cards.content: This key starts a new line or confirms what you have typed.

cards.question: You want to add a space between two words. Which key do you press?
You typed the wrong letter by mistake. Which key removes it?

summaryPoints: A keyboard has letter keys, a space bar, a backspace key, and an enter key.
We press one key at a time carefully to type words.
homeworkItems: If there is a keyboard at home, practise finding and pressing the letters in your name.

teachingScript.overview: Use a real keyboard (or a large printed keyboard picture if devices are limited) and let children physically point to and press keys as each part is introduced.

talkingPoints: Show a real keyboard and point out that letters are not always in alphabetical order.
Have children find the space bar and backspace on a real or printed keyboard as each is introduced.
Ask children to point to the correct key before answering.
Give each child a turn to type their own name carefully, one letter at a time.
misconceptions: Children may press keys very fast without looking -- encourage slow, careful, one-letter-at-a-time typing at this stage.

quizQuestions.question: Which key adds a space between words?
Which key removes the last letter you typed?

flashcards.definition: A set of keys used to type letters, numbers, and words on a computer or tablet.
The long key at the bottom of a keyboard used to add a space between words.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Using a Keyboard
worksheetContent.instructions: Answer the questions about the keyboard.

questions.prompt: Which key would you press to add a space between two words?
Which key helps you fix a typing mistake?
Write your name in capital letters, one letter per box.

unit-2.title: Staying Safe and Well Online
unit-2.description: Keeping ourselves safe on devices, asking a trusted adult for help, and taking care of ourselves while using screens.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 -- Keeping Ourselves Safe on Devices
lessons.objectives: Understand that some information (like your full name, address, or password) should stay private; recognise that devices are used with permission.
lessons.syllabusRef: Safety and wellbeing -- Staying safe online

steps.title: Keeping information private
steps.definition: Some information about us is private, which means we only share it with people we know and trust, like our family and teachers -- not with a device or a game, and not with strangers.
steps.example: A game might ask for your address to "unlock a prize" -- private information like this should stay with a trusted grown-up, not typed into a device.

steps.title: Private or okay to share with the class?
categories: Okay to share with the class

items.label: Your home address
items.reason: Your address is private information that should only be shared with trusted adults.

items.label: Your favourite colour
items.correctCategory: Okay to share with the class
items.reason: This is a fun fact about you that isn't private information.

items.label: Your device password
items.reason: A password should stay private so only you (and a trusted adult) can use your account.

items.label: Your favourite animal
items.correctCategory: Okay to share with the class
items.reason: This is a fun fact about you that isn't private information.

summaryPoints: Information like your address and passwords should stay private.
We only use devices with permission from a grown-up or teacher.
homeworkItems: Ask a grown-up at home what information they think should always stay private.

teachingScript.overview: Keep examples concrete and age-appropriate -- focus on 'private vs. shareable' as a simple sorting skill rather than discussing online strangers or risk in detail, which is not appropriate for this age group.

talkingPoints: Use a simple, reassuring tone -- the goal is a habit, not fear.
Discuss each item as a group before sorting it, so reasoning is shared out loud.
misconceptions: Children may think all personal facts are private -- clarify that fun facts like favourite colour are fine to share, while an address or password is different.

talkingPoints: Reassure children that a trusted adult is always the right person to ask if unsure.

quizQuestions.question: Which of these should stay private?
Who should you ask before using a device?

flashcards.definition: Information that should only be shared with people you know and trust.
A secret set of letters or numbers that keeps an account safe -- it should stay private.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Keeping Information Private
worksheetContent.instructions: Sort the pieces of information into private and okay to share.

questions.prompt: Name one piece of information that should stay private.
questions.answer: For example: your home address or a password.

questions.prompt: Who should you ask before using a device?
Draw a trusted grown-up you could ask for help with a device.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 -- Asking a Trusted Adult for Help
lessons.objectives: Identify trusted adults who can help with devices; recognise situations where you should ask for help.
lessons.syllabusRef: Safety and wellbeing -- Staying safe online

steps.title: Asking a trusted adult
steps.definition: A trusted adult is someone you know well who looks after you, like a parent, carer, or teacher. If something on a device confuses you, worries you, or you don't know what to do, you ask a trusted adult for help.
steps.example: If a pop-up appears on the screen that you don't understand, you stop and show it to your teacher instead of tapping on it.

cards.question: A strange message pops up on the screen. What should you do?
cards.answer: Stop and show it to a trusted adult, like your teacher.

cards.question: You forget how to save your picture. What should you do?
cards.answer: Ask your teacher or a trusted adult to help you.

cards.question: You want to draw a picture using colours you already know how to use. Do you need to ask for help?
cards.answer: Not necessarily -- but it's always fine to ask if you're ever unsure.

summaryPoints: A trusted adult is someone who looks after you, like a parent, carer, or teacher.
If something on a device confuses or worries you, stop and ask a trusted adult.
homeworkItems: Tell a grown-up at home who your trusted adults are at school and at home.

teachingScript.overview: Role-play a simple scenario (an unexpected pop-up or message) so children practise the physical action of stopping and telling a teacher, not just the words.

talkingPoints: Name the trusted adults present in the room right now (teacher, teaching assistant) as concrete examples.
Act out the 'stop and show a trusted adult' response as a physical routine the class practises together.
Ask each child to name one trusted adult at home and one at school.

quizQuestions.question: If something on a screen confuses you, you should...
Which of these is a trusted adult?

flashcards.definition: Someone who looks after you and you can go to for help, like a parent, carer, or teacher.
To tell a trusted adult when you are unsure, confused, or worried about something.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Trusted Adults
worksheetContent.instructions: Draw and answer the questions about trusted adults.

questions.prompt: Name one trusted adult who could help you with a device.
questions.answer: For example: a parent, carer, or teacher.

questions.prompt: What should you do if something on a screen worries you?
questions.answer: Stop and tell a trusted adult.

questions.prompt: Draw a trusted adult at home and one at school.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 -- Taking Breaks and Looking After Ourselves
lessons.objectives: Understand why taking breaks from screens is important; recognise simple signs it's time for a break.

steps.title: Taking breaks from screens
steps.definition: Looking at a screen for a long time can make our eyes tired and our bodies stiff, so it's healthy to take breaks -- stretch, look at something far away, or go outside for a while.
steps.example: After using a tablet for a while, we stand up, stretch our arms, and look out of the window at something far away to rest our eyes.

steps.title: Ways to take a healthy break

cards.label: Stretch
cards.content: Standing up and stretching helps our body after sitting still.

cards.label: Look far away
cards.content: Looking at something far away, like a tree outside, gives our eyes a rest.

cards.label: Drink some water
cards.content: Taking a break to drink water keeps us feeling good.

cards.label: Go outside
cards.content: Playing outside for a while balances out time spent on a screen.

questions.question: Why is it healthy to take breaks from a screen?
options: To rest our eyes and body
questions.feedback: ✓ Breaks help rest our eyes and body.

questions.question: Which of these is a good way to take a break?
questions.feedback: ✓ Looking far away helps rest our eyes.

summaryPoints: Taking breaks from screens helps rest our eyes and body.
We can stretch, look far away, drink water, or go outside during a break.
homeworkItems: Practise taking a short break -- stretch and look at something far away -- after screen time at home.

teachingScript.overview: Physically lead the class through a short stretch-and-look-far-away break during the lesson, so the habit is practised, not just discussed.

talkingPoints: Ask children how their eyes or body feel after looking at something closely for a long time.
Actually do each break idea together as a class as it is revealed.
Ask children to explain why in their own words, not just choose an answer.
End the lesson with one full class stretch-and-look-far-away break.

quizQuestions.question: Why should we take breaks from screens?
options: To rest our eyes and body
Screens need a rest, not us

quizQuestions.question: Which of these helps rest your eyes during a break?
options: Closing your eyes and holding the device

flashcards.definition: A short pause from an activity, like screen time, to rest and look after yourself.
Looking after how our body and mind feel.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Taking Healthy Breaks
worksheetContent.instructions: Answer the questions about taking breaks from screens.

questions.prompt: Name two ways to take a healthy break from a screen.
questions.answer: For example: stretching and looking at something far away.

questions.prompt: Why is it good to look at something far away during a break?
Draw yourself taking a healthy break -- stretching, drinking water, or playing outside.

unit-3.title: Understanding Technology Around Us
unit-3.description: Noticing the technology we use every day and how it helps people do things and communicate.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 -- Technology We Use Every Day
lessons.objectives: Identify examples of technology used at home, at school, and in the community; describe what each one helps us do.
lessons.syllabusRef: Understanding the digital world -- Technology in everyday life

steps.title: Technology all around us
steps.definition: Technology means tools people have made to help us do things. Some technology uses electricity and digital parts, like a computer or a phone; some is simpler, like a bicycle.
steps.example: A rice cooker is technology that helps a family cook rice without watching a pot the whole time.

steps.title: What does it help us do?

cards.definition: Helps people talk to and message each other, even far away.
Helps people write, learn, and find information.
Helps keep people safe by controlling when cars and people can go.
Helps cook rice safely without needing to watch it the whole time.

steps.title: Where do we usually see this technology?

items.label: Rice cooker
items.reason: A rice cooker is usually found in a kitchen at home.

items.label: Classroom computer
items.reason: Classroom computers are used for learning at school.

items.label: Traffic light
items.reason: Traffic lights are found on roads in the community.

items.label: Television
items.reason: A television is usually found in a living room at home.

summaryPoints: Technology is a tool people have made to help us do things.
We can find technology at home, at school, and in the community.
homeworkItems: Find three examples of technology at home and tell a grown-up what each one helps you do.

teachingScript.overview: Where possible, bring in or point to real, familiar examples from the children's own lives at home and around the school and village, rather than only unfamiliar or foreign examples.

talkingPoints: Start by asking children to name one piece of technology they saw this morning.
Ask children to guess what each item helps us do before flipping the card.
Discuss that some technology, like a phone, could belong in more than one place -- focus on where it is most commonly found.
misconceptions: Children may think only screens count as technology -- clarify that simple tools like traffic lights and rice cookers count too.

talkingPoints: Ask a few children to share the technology example they will look for at home.

quizQuestions.question: What does the word 'technology' mean?
options: A tool people have made to help us do things

quizQuestions.question: Where would you usually find a traffic light?

flashcards.definition: A tool people have made to help us do things, such as a computer, a rice cooker, or a traffic light.
Something that happens or is used regularly, most days.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Technology We Use Every Day
worksheetContent.instructions: Look at each picture and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Name one piece of technology you use at home.
questions.answer: Answers will vary, e.g. a television or a rice cooker.

questions.prompt: Name one piece of technology you use at school.
Draw one piece of technology and write what it helps you do.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 -- How Technology Helps Us Communicate
lessons.objectives: Identify ways people use technology to communicate with others, including over distance; compare talking in person to using technology to communicate.
lessons.syllabusRef: Understanding the digital world -- Communication technology

steps.title: Communicating with technology
steps.definition: Communication means sharing information or feelings with others. Technology like phones and video calls helps people communicate even when they are far apart, not just when they are in the same room.
steps.example: A video call lets a child show their grandparent, who lives far away, a picture they have drawn -- even though they are not in the same place.

cards.question: You want to talk to a friend sitting next to you. Do you need technology?
cards.answer: No -- you can simply talk to them in person.

cards.question: You want to show a drawing to a family member who lives far away. What could help?
cards.answer: A phone or video call could let them see it, even from far away.

cards.question: Is talking to someone face-to-face still a good way to communicate, even with technology available?
cards.answer: Yes -- talking in person is often the best way to communicate when we are together.

summaryPoints: Communication means sharing information or feelings with others.
Technology like phones and video calls can help us communicate with people who are far away.
homeworkItems: Ask a grown-up about a time they used technology to communicate with someone far away.

teachingScript.overview: Keep the comparison balanced -- technology is a helpful tool for distance, but talking in person remains valuable and is not being replaced.

talkingPoints: Ask if any child has family who live far away and how they keep in touch.
Discuss each scenario as a group, drawing out the reasoning before revealing the answer.
Reinforce that both in-person talking and technology are valuable ways to communicate, used in different situations.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'communicate' mean?
options: To share information or feelings with others

quizQuestions.question: Which of these could help you talk to a family member who lives far away?

flashcards.definition: To share information or feelings with another person, such as by talking or messaging.
A way of using technology to see and talk to someone who is in a different place.

questions.prompt: Name one way technology can help you talk to someone far away.
questions.answer: For example: a phone call or a video call.

questions.prompt: Is talking in person still a good way to communicate? Why?
questions.answer: Yes -- it is often the best way to communicate when people are together.

questions.prompt: Draw yourself communicating with someone, in person or using technology.
